analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts permanent and pays for protecting defense by cutting food stamps, Medicaid, and Wall Street rules.
analysis.headline: Representative Jim Jordan's fiscal-cliff bill, introduced December 19, 2012 with 22 Republican cosponsors, was referred to nine committees and never received a vote before the 112th Congress ended two weeks later.
analysis.plain_summary: In December 2012, just before across-the-board tax increases and spending cuts were set to hit, Representative Jim Jordan offered this package. It would make every one of the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts permanent, including the top income rates, lower capital gains rates, and estate tax relief. To pay for replacing scheduled defense cuts, it cuts food stamp benefits, Medicaid and children's health insurance protections, federal employee retirement, and rolls back Wall Street reforms including the consumer bureau's funding and the power to wind down failing big financial firms. It also caps jury awards in medical malpractice cases. The bill went nowhere: it was split among nine committees, none acted, and Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Top-earning households keep the 35% top rate permanently and the 15% rate on capital gains and dividends; wealthy estates keep the 2010 law's estate tax terms through 2013. Corporations and high-income small-business owners would benefit from a fast-track process for a tax overhaul with a top individual and corporate rate of 25% and a shift to a territorial system. Financial institutions gain from repeal of Dodd-Frank's orderly liquidation authority, putting the consumer bureau under annual appropriations, and eliminating the Office of Financial Research. Health care providers and medical product makers gain from a $250,000 cap on noneconomic damages and a shield from punitive damages for FDA-approved products. Defense spending is shielded from the harshest part of the sequester. Middle-income households also gain from a larger alternative minimum tax exemption and $100,000 small-business expensing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, wealthy estates, banks, doctors, defense

how_it_helps.text: Makes the 2001 tax cuts permanent and permanently keeps the reduced rates on capital gains and dividends from the 2003 act, with estate and gift tax relief extended through 2013.
Extends the increased alternative minimum tax exemption for 2012 and 2013 and raises the small-business expensing allowance to $100,000 for 2013.

Replaces the scheduled January 2, 2013 sequester with a smaller $19.104 billion across-the-board discretionary cut, removes veterans' medical care from sequester, and nullifies any defense direct-spending sequester.

Sets a fast-track process for a 2013 tax reform bill requiring at most two individual brackets (10% and no higher than 25%), a corporate rate no higher than 25%, repeal of the AMT, revenue held between 18% and 19% of the economy, and a territorial tax system.

Caps noneconomic damages in health care lawsuits at $250,000, restricts attorney contingency fees, requires clear and convincing evidence of malicious intent for punitive damages, and shields FDA-approved medical products and their prescribers from punitive damages.

analysis.who_pays: Food stamp recipients: states would lose the option to use broader categorical eligibility, households receiving only non-cash state benefits could be dropped, the LIHEAP-related utility deduction is narrowed, the boosted benefit levels for Puerto Rico and American Samoa end immediately, and employment and training funding falls from $90 million to $79 million. Medicaid and CHIP beneficiaries in states that want to cut eligibility lose the federal maintenance-of-effort requirement; territory Medicaid funding drops. Federal employees face retirement contributions rising by 5% of salary over five years (8.5% for Members of Congress), and new hires lose the FERS annuity supplement. Homeowners lose new HAMP mortgage modification help. The consumer bureau's independent funding is replaced with annual congressional appropriations, and the power to wind down failing financial companies is repealed. States lose the Title XX social services block grant program. Medical malpractice victims with severe injuries bear the damage caps.
analysis.who_pays_short: Food stamp, Medicaid, and federal-worker households

drawbacks.text: The bill finances permanent upper-income tax rates with cuts concentrated on low-income programs: SNAP categorical eligibility would be limited to households receiving cash assistance, the standard utility allowance linked to energy assistance would be narrowed, and the Recovery Act benefit increase for Puerto Rico and American Samoa would end immediately.

Repealing Medicaid and CHIP maintenance-of-effort protections would let states cut eligibility levels for children and low-income adults, and repeal of the Prevention and Public Health Fund and state exchange establishment grants would strip funding from the Affordable Care Act's coverage and prevention programs.

Ending Dodd-Frank's orderly liquidation authority would return to bankruptcy as the only path for failing nonbank financial firms, the mechanism Congress created after the 2008 crisis in part to avoid disorderly collapses of firms like Lehman Brothers; putting the consumer bureau under annual appropriations would expose its funding to the very industry it polices, and the Office of Financial Research would be abolished.

A $250,000 cap on noneconomic damages falls hardest on patients with the most severe injuries, such as children, retirees, and people who cannot show lost wages, since pain and suffering is their main recoverable loss.
The tax reform fast-track locks in a revenue ceiling of 18-19% of the economy and bars Senate amendments from being debated beyond short time limits, limiting lawmakers' ability to modify the plan.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real near-term relief, chiefly AMT fixes and protection of middle-class tax rates, and its authors correctly note the tax code's complexity. But its central feature is making upper-income tax rates permanent while the offsetting cuts fall on food assistance, Medicaid, children's health protections, federal workers, and consumer financial enforcement. The malpractice caps and FDA liability shield shift risk from providers and manufacturers onto injured patients. HAMP's poor performance, which the bill's own findings document, supports ending that one program, but the rest of the package is a transfer of resources and legal protections toward higher-income households and regulated industries.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced two weeks before the fiscal cliff deadline, the bill was referred to nine House committees, none of which acted, and the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 without the bill ever getting a vote.

narrative.text: Representative Jim Jordan introduced the Averting the Fiscal Cliff Act on December 19, 2012, joined by 22 cosponsors, all Republicans.
The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and eight other committees, and a portion was referred to the Health Subcommittee.
No committee acted on the bill, and its last entry in the congressional record is the initial referral, with no vote ever held before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
The bill would have made the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts permanent, including the reduced rates on capital gains and dividends, and extended estate tax relief through 2013.

Its offsetting cuts included narrowed food stamp eligibility, termination of boosted SNAP benefits for Puerto Rico and American Samoa, repeal of Medicaid and CHIP maintenance-of-effort protections, and repeal of the Title XX social services block grant.

It would have repealed Dodd-Frank's orderly liquidation authority and the Office of Financial Research, placed the consumer bureau under annual appropriations, and terminated the HAMP mortgage modification program, which the bill's findings say saved about $2.84 billion according to the Congressional Budget Office.
It would have replaced the scheduled sequester with a $19.104 billion across-the-board discretionary cut while nullifying any defense direct-spending sequester for fiscal year 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, food stamp and Medicaid recipients, federal workers, homeowners counting on mortgage modification help, and consumers relying on the consumer bureau's independent funding kept the existing law, and high-income households and large financial firms did not get the permanent tax rates and deregulation the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Benefit recipients and consumers kept existing law

for.name: Rep. Jim Jordan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 19, 2012, combining permanent extension of the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts with a sequester-replacement package of spending and regulation cuts.

for.name: 22 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors of the bill.

for.name: House Republican Study Committee
for.what_they_did: Backed the package as the conservative bloc's alternative for addressing the fiscal cliff, with Jordan as its chair.

against.name: Nine House committees
against.role: Ways and Means, Budget, Agriculture, Energy and Commerce, Financial Services, Judiciary, Oversight and Government Reform, House Administration, Rules
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on December 19, 2012 and took no further action before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Opposed making all of the 2001 and 2003 tax cuts permanent and the package's cuts to food stamps, Medicaid, and financial regulation during the fiscal cliff negotiations.

against.name: President Obama
against.what_they_did: Pressed for a fiscal cliff deal that let the high-income tax cuts expire rather than extending all of them, making a bill extending everything permanent politically impossible.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support, and the fiscal cliff dispute that year split along party lines over whether high-income tax cuts should be extended.

industries.note: The bill makes the 35% top income rate, the 15% capital gains and dividend rates, and the 2010 estate tax terms permanent or extended, financed by cuts to food stamps, Medicaid protections, and social services block grants.

Repeal of Dodd-Frank's orderly liquidation authority and the Office of Financial Research, plus subjecting the consumer bureau to annual appropriations, removes the funding and resolution rules the 2008-crisis law imposed.

industries.industry: Health care providers and medical product manufacturers
industries.note: A $250,000 cap on noneconomic damages, limits on punitive damages, an FDA-compliance shield, and caps on contingency fees reduce their liability exposure, with the cost falling on severely injured patients.
The bill nullifies the fiscal 2013 defense sequester and replaces it with a smaller across-the-board cut, sparing defense the largest scheduled reductions.

industries.industry: Health insurers and nonprofit CO-OP plans
industries.note: Repeal of Affordable Care Act grants for state exchanges and rescission of CO-OP program funds cut the ACA funding stream that supported exchange establishment and new nonprofit issuers.
HAMP's termination ends the federal modification subsidy, while a sense-of-Congress provision asks banks to work with homeowners voluntarily.
